lead: The engine runs shows for any game, not only ALN. This site starts from its ten promises: what each person can count on, when, and what must happen for them. The other pages hold what is open for you to decide, the ten promises in full, the parts of one candidate shape for the whole engine, the design flaws that break promises today, and a change log of earlier wordings.

open: Thirteen questions wait for you on [[page:decisions]], in four groups; answer in the chat by the question's letter or number.

About the promises: eight. Whether these are the right ten, each said from the side of the people who count on it, and whether one is missing ([[q:promises]]); then A to G on their wording and whether three of them should split ([[q:A]] to [[q:G]]). The relationship map changed the recommendations for E, F and G.

About standalone games: three. The hardware scanner's standalone mode under your parity rule ([[q:22]]), one GM tablet per standalone game ([[q:24]]), and what exposed evidence and video tokens do with no engine and no TV ([[q:25]]).
About the game's record: one. Whether a refused GM scan is kept in the game's record ([[q:19]]).
About the next step: one. How many problems the test rig proves before design starts ([[q:21]]).
decided: Decision 29 (2026-11-01): the owner page becomes five linked pages and a change log, all built from one set of data.

Decision 28 (2026-11-01): the after-game article and emailer. The night's-record half of [[promise:J3]] names the director and the players; what the players receive after the show is the game's business; the night's record carries the game it ran and the texts the players saw; players' emails stay outside the engine; ALN's Director Console stays a separate program that reads the record, with room to run inside the Review stage later; the two clocks join [[flaw:C9]].

Decision 27 (2026-11-01): the words. A promise is what a person can count on at a given moment; parts keep promises; design flaws break them; a quality is something every part must have; promises go by their titles, never by number; the person who fits a kit to a venue is the venue technician.
next: Step 2 rebuilds the test rig, the automated machine with real video, music, audio and lighting stand-ins that was lost with the old container, and proves the design flaws on it for real instead of reading them off the code. How many it proves first is [[q:21]].

Step 3 designs rule by rule, with competing designs side by side for each choice listed on [[page:decisions]] under coming in step 3. Each rule's page joins this site and links back to the promises, parts and flaws here.
This site replaces version 7 at the same link; earlier versions are in the [[page:changes]].

moments.name: Author and Rehearse
moments.when: In the days before a show, on a laptop or on the show machine between games, when a designer builds a game, changes a value, publishes and plays a round.
people: The game designer
The owner, designing the second game
A new designer, learning from the toy game
The designer reading a badge on a draft

promises.why: Build a game or change one value in it, publish and apply it, and play a round within minutes; the engine's own check refuses a bad pack at the desk; nothing done here can reach the live show or its records.
The badge on a draft uses the same go and no-go words as the show, and a desk check never passes for a room check.
Designers reach their tools and only those.

moments.name: Before doors
moments.when: In the days before an event and at doors-open, when the venue technician fits the game to the venue and the preflight answers go or no-go.
people: The venue technician
The GM at doors-open
A future operator with a second kit
A stranger on the venue wifi

promises.why: The venue technician states what the kit brings tonight, binds the pack's names to real instruments and gets one go or no-go; a second kit or a new machine needs no change to engine code.
The venue technician's go is a go: every line says paper or live, and a desk check never passes for a room check.
Every tablet and scanner holds the same copy of the pack, and the GM sees at a glance that they match, or a mismatched device is refused.
Venue technicians reach their tools and only those; a stranger on the venue wifi sees nothing.

moments.name: During play
moments.when: Mid-show, at every tap on a token or a button, every command and every glance at a screen; also on a night when the game runs with no engine by choice.
people: The GM running the live show: at a token, a button, the start and pause buttons, or the Environment and Show Control sections
The players, each at a token, with no account
The audience, reading the TV and watching the clock
In future games, a player with a hidden fact
A GM running a game with no engine
A stranger on the venue wifi

promises.why: At a tap on a token or a button, the GM or the player learns at once whether it counted, why not if it did not, or that it is held for later or must be tried again; nothing is silently lost or doubled.
Whatever the GM did on any tablet is what every tablet, the TV and the audience see, also after a tablet comes back; in future games a player's hidden fact reaches only its owner.
The room does what the designer cued and what the GM asked; the GM sees it happen, or sees at once that it did not and what to press; a dead program comes back by itself before anyone notices.
A pause blocks scans, and a restart during a show loses nothing.

The GM alone can start, pause, end and change scores, and the engine knows which tablet did it; the audience sees scores and exposed evidence and nothing else; a player sees the memory they scanned; a stranger sees nothing.
Red means act now, grey means absent on purpose, old looks old, and the TV's clock never counts on its own.
A game declared standalone knows it is standalone instead of showing a lost connection all night.
No test or rehearsal ever reaches a live show.

moments.name: The end of a game, and between games
moments.when: When the GM ends or resets a game and before the next one starts; the designer's publish lands here, and a pack change is taken up only here.
people: The GM who ends and resets games
The designer who publishes a game, or a second designer later

promises.why: An ended game stays ended and no scan lands in it; the next game starts clean; a between-games edit never reaches the game in progress.
The whole kit plays the game the designer published, that version, with no code change; a second designer's game runs on the same engine.
The designer publishes and applies a change between games, and the live show never notices.

moments.name: Review
moments.when: After the game, when the night is reviewed and told.
people: The director who tells the night's story
The players it is told to
The owner and the designer

promises.why: The director tells the players the story of their night from what was captured during play, with the game and the texts they saw, not reconstructed; how that story reaches the players is the game's own business.

moments.name: Release day
moments.when: Before every change reaches anyone, and on the day the owner sends a new version to the venue.
people: The developer changing the engine
The owner sending a version to the venue

promises.why: When every test passes, the show still runs for ALN and for the toy game; the owner decides when a new version goes to the venue, the machine carries one matching set, and the owner can swap back by replugging a machine.

standaloneLine: Decision 22 adds a requirement to every promise: a whole game can run with no engine, the GM tablet and the player scanners each working alone, as a choice the game declares, and no game mixes networked and standalone devices. Each promise and each card says what changes with no engine; the standalone pass, with the hardware scanner's parity table, is on [[page:flaws]].

fitSummary.head: What happens at every tap.
fitSummary.text: In the candidate shape, four promises meet at every tap in a networked game. The designer's pack sets the rules, which [[part:P1]] alone calculates ([[promise:J1]]). The [[part:P3]], the same on every screen, is what the tap is judged against ([[promise:J2]]). The request comes in through [[part:P4]], the one door in, and the answer goes back to the GM or the player; an accepted tap joins the record ([[promise:J3]]). [[part:P7]] say who tapped and who may see the result ([[promise:J7]]). Every fact that changed then goes out through [[part:P6]], the one door out, to every screen that may see it, with its label: what it is, how old, how sure.

fitSummary.head: The engine's own machinery.
fitSummary.text: [[part:P8]] reports what each program in the room is doing, dated. [[part:P10]] turns that, and the venue technician's profile in [[part:P12]], into go, no-go or "not installed tonight" ([[promise:J8]], [[promise:J9]]). [[part:P9]] holds the cues, the clock, the video queue and the items held while a service is down, so the room does what was cued and asked ([[promise:J4]]). [[part:P11]] says when to check again and what each part resets at setup, start, pause, end, reset, restart and the next game, which feeds back into the equipment ([[promise:J5]]); it alone moves a game, and it takes up a new pack only between games. The profile feeds this loop from outside. In today's code the loop is also a chain of seven backend modules that depend on each other in a circle, with the game's record caught inside it.

fitSummary.head: What reaches the show from outside.
fitSummary.text: In the candidate, the designer's week and the developer's proof reach a live show only through the pack and through each engine having its own names. [[part:P15]] talks to the engine by message, and its publish travels down [[part:P2]], one list of every holder of the pack with a version stamp on every copy ([[promise:J6]]). [[part:P13]] gives each engine its own data folder, ports, process files and passes, so a test, a preview or a second kit never touches the live one; [[part:P16]] run on an engine of their own and on two packs, and [[part:P17]] compares what a machine carries against one described set ([[promise:J10]]).

fitSummary.head: The night's record, after the end.
fitSummary.text: In the candidate, when the GM ends a game, [[part:P11]] closes it and [[part:P5]] writes one record of the night from the facts the engine decided, with the roster, notes, accusation and photos captured into it during play, stamped with the game it ran and the texts the players saw. The director tells the players the story of their night from it, and the owner and the designer read it too: the second half of [[promise:J3]]. The designer's Review stage reads it inside the engine; for ALN the Director Console, a separate program, reads it from outside, with room to move inside the Review stage later (decision 28). Today nothing writes this record; the tablet builds a report from its own copies.

around.name: Notion
around.what: The database where ALN's memories are written: each token's text, its rating, its type and its group.
around.connects: The sync script reads it and writes the pack files. The engine never reads Notion; it takes the game only from the pack. ALN's Director Console still reads memory texts here, not from the pack the game ran.
around.status: Today's source for ALN's content. Paper documents are not in the pack at all; whether they join it, with "unlocked" recorded during play, is a question for step 3 (decision 28).

around.name: The sync script
around.what: A Python script that turns the Notion database into the pack's token file, derives the group multipliers from Notion's authoring shorthand, draws the display images and regenerates the pack manifest.
around.connects: Its output is the pack files folder; in the candidate it is one source of the pack that [[part:P2]] adopts, and nothing else in the engine knows it exists.
around.status: Today. It is one of the nine holders of the pack that nothing joins ([[flaw:C12]]).

around.name: The pack files
around.what: The shared folder of token definitions, the rules file (scoring, modes, groups, the duplicate policy, the game clock) and a manifest with a fingerprint of the whole.
around.connects: The engine freezes a snapshot of it at boot; the GM tablet and the phone carry nested copies; the hardware scanner downloads it from the engine. In the candidate [[part:P2]] is the one list of holders, one notice that the pack changed, and a version stamp every copy shows and every game record carries; [[part:P1]] takes its rules only from here.
around.status: Today the pack is held in nine places and no message says it changed, so after a publish the TV, the engine and a tablet can run three versions of one game ([[flaw:C12]], [[flaw:C14]]).

around.name: The design studio, today the config tool
around.what: The designer's drafts and their publishing, and the venue technician's profile editor, in a web tool beside the engine.
around.connects: Today it writes the engine's settings, routing file and media folders, imports engine modules by path and runs the engine's pack check as a child process; an edit shows at the engine's next restart. In the candidate [[part:P15]] talks to the engine only by message, applies at a window the lifecycle allows, and rehearses on a preview engine kept apart by [[part:P13]].
around.status: Today, with [[flaw:C12]] and [[flaw:C8]]. Whether it stays a separate program or becomes a surface the engine itself serves is a choice for step 3.

around.name: Video and the TV
around.what: VLC, which plays the show's videos on the TV, and the TV's browser, which shows the scoreboard page.
around.connects: Both sit behind [[part:P8]] as adapters; [[part:P9]] queues videos and holds one while the player is busy or down. The browser is also a client of the engine under a watch-only pass, and the engine launches, shows, hides and kills it as an outside program.
around.status: Today the engine's picture of VLC carries no age and is re-read only in part ([[flaw:C3]]); the scoreboard page decides which modes count as evidence from a file it fetched ([[flaw:C12]]). One interface per capability or per program is a choice for step 3.

around.name: Music
around.what: MPD, the music player, with its playlists.
around.connects: An adapter behind [[part:P8]]; the show runner ducks it under a video or a sound.
around.status: Today it keeps a private connected flag beside the shared health list, and its panel can keep a calm playing look while the engine knows the player is down ([[flaw:C2]]).

around.name: Audio and Bluetooth
around.what: PipeWire, which routes video, music and sounds to the HDMI or the Bluetooth sink and sets each volume; the sound player; and BlueZ, which pairs and connects the Bluetooth speaker.
around.connects: Adapters behind [[part:P8]]; the venue technician's profile in [[part:P12]] says which sink is which.
around.status: Today seven adapters with no shared interface above them and two supervision shapes ([[flaw:C3]]); the tests adopt the live audio and Bluetooth ([[flaw:C8]]).

around.name: Lighting
around.what: Home Assistant, which holds the scenes the designer's cues name.
around.connects: An adapter behind [[part:P8]]; a scene name in the pack binds to a real scene through [[part:P12]].
around.status: Today the lighting panel stays unavailable until a reload if Home Assistant was down at engine start ([[flaw:C2]]). On the test rig a witness light per lighting role stands in for the room.

around.name: The after-game article: ALN's Director Console
around.what: A web app on the director's Windows computer, outside the kit. An AI writing pipeline waits at eleven stops for the director, who marks which paper documents the players unlocked, gives the roster with pronouns, pastes the accusation, the GM tablet's report and notes, picks and edits the story, names who is in each photo and approves the article, published as a web page two to eleven days after the game.
around.connects: Today it parses the tablet's downloaded markdown report with an AI call, reads memory texts and paper documents from Notion rather than the pack the game ran, takes the roster, notes and photos by hand, and shifts money events stamped by two clocks back into line ([[flaw:C9]]). In the candidate it reads [[part:P5]], which carries the pack the game ran and the texts the players saw, so the article quotes what they held.
around.status: Decided (28): plan for the console staying a separate program that reads the engine's record, and design the record so the console can later become ALN's own part of the engine's Review stage.

around.name: The emailer
around.what: An interactive script on the same computer. The director pastes the booking list, an optional note and a photo folder; it sends each player a thank-you email from the game's Gmail account with the article link, the feedback form link for that date, a return-visit discount code and the photos, and keeps a list of who was sent what on that computer.
around.connects: Outside the engine. It reads the article's address and the booking list, and nothing from the engine or the night's record.
around.status: Decided (28): what the players receive after the show is the game's business, and the engine makes them no promise of their own.

around.name: The booking list and the ticketing service
around.what: Each player's name and email, from the bookings for a date.
around.connects: Pasted into the emailer by the director today. It never enters the engine: a player taps tokens with no account, no login and no recorded identity unless the game designs an identification moment, and players' data stays on the kit.
around.status: Decided (28): players' emails stay outside the engine. Later the game's own tools could collect them from the ticketing service's API.

siteGuide.line: The whole engine in one read, and the way to every other page; start here.
Everything open for you, each question with its evidence on the same screen; answer in the chat by the question's letter or number.
The requirements: what each person counts on, when, with what is built today, the long-term goal, the parts that keep each promise and the flaws that break it.
The candidate design: seventeen parts in layers, five moments followed through them, which part would run where, and where a real alternative exists; the frame step 3 starts from.
What breaks the promises today: one card per flaw with its evidence, grouped under the promise each mainly breaks, with the standalone pass and the parity table.
Earlier wordings, what changed on each promise and card and why, the recommendations the map changed, and the words decision 27 replaced.

words.def: What a person can count on at a given moment. Parts keep promises; design flaws break them.
When a promise matters: a production stage (Author, Rehearse, Run, Review), a point in a show, or release day.
Something in today's design that breaks a promise.
One of the 17 pieces of the candidate design. It runs on the engine or on a device.
Something every part must have so a promise holds everywhere, like honest or proven. It keeps promises; it is never a promise or a part.
The person who tells the night's story at the Review stage and carries what was learned back into Author; usually the same person as the GM or the designer.
Checked from the files only, or checked against the equipment in the room.
What a device shows when it connects: who it is and what it may do.
Grey, absent on purpose, never a fault. The code calls it dormant.
Any piece of code with an inside and an outside, from one function to the whole backend.
Everything other code must know to use a module.
Where one module meets another, and where behaviour can be swapped.
A deep module does a lot behind a small interface. A shallow one makes its callers know almost as much as it does.
A fix in one place fixes it everywhere.
The real thing plugged in at a seam, like VLC behind "play a video".

promises: A promise is what a person can count on at a given moment. These ten are the engine's requirements, each said from the side of the people who count on it: who, when, and what must happen for them. The table at the top gives all ten at a glance with the parts that would keep each and the design flaws that break it; the two diagrams under it show how the promises depend on each other, the second folded. Whether these are the right ten, and whether three of them should split, is [[q:promises]] and A to G on [[page:decisions]].

Each entry reads the same way. The title is the promise. Who and when name the people and the moment. What they count on is the promise in full. Built today says what already exists for it. The long-term goal is where the design is heading; where it is marked open, step 3 settles it. Kept by names the parts of the candidate shape that would keep it, each a link to [[page:parts]]. Broken by lists the design flaws that break it today, the main one first, each with one line on how; the cards are on [[page:flaws]]. In a standalone game says what changes with no engine. Folded under the entry are what the planned capabilities need from it and the test cases taken from the shows.
The promises wait for your confirmation; the parts named under each are a candidate. Each promise's earlier wording, and what the relationship map changed, are on [[page:changes]].
parts: This is a candidate shape for the whole engine, not a decision. Most of today's problems sit in work several promises depend on: getting a fact onto a screen, answering a request, knowing who is connected, the boundary between one game and the next. Each is done several times today, in different places. In the candidate each such piece of work becomes one part, seventeen in all, and the parts already well built today (the game rules, the verdict, the health words) are the pattern for the rest. Step 3 starts from this frame and puts competing designs in front of you; where the map found two sound ways, the last table on this page names both and what each costs.

Each part has a card. What it does says the part's work in plain words. Mainly keeps names the promises the part exists for, and also needed by the promises that use it; each is a link to [[page:promises]]. Today says how the same work is done now, and removes names the design flaws the part would take away, each a link to [[page:flaws]]. Runs on says which devices would host it: the engine, GM tablets, player scanners, the scoreboards, the config tool or the tests; in a standalone game several parts run as small stand-ins on the GM tablet. Where it can be swapped names the part's seams: what plugs into it, and where behaviour can change without touching the rest.

Before the cards come the qualities every part must have, the parts in layers (each part uses only the parts in the rows below it, so nothing loops back) and five moments at a show followed through the parts in order. After them come which part would run where, the tangles where today's code spreads one piece of work over many places, and the choices where a real alternative exists.
flaws: A design flaw is something in today's design that breaks a promise. There are sixteen, C1 to C16, and one proposed, N1, which [[q:C]] asks about. Each has one promise it mainly breaks, and its card sits under that promise's heading; where a flaw also breaks other promises, those entries on [[page:promises]] point back to the card. The table at the top gives every flaw at a glance, with the promises it breaks, the parts that would remove it, how many findings sit under it and whether it was seen live.

A card tells one moment at a show, then why it happens. Two diagrams follow. Today shows how the problem happens now, with the place it goes wrong drawn in red. Candidate, not decided shows how the candidate shape would remove it, with the one place that would own the fact drawn in teal. The card then names the parts that would remove it, each a link to [[page:parts]], and restates the reason in design terms: modules, interfaces, seams, locality. In a standalone game says what the flaw does with no engine, today and in the candidate. The problems behind it lists the findings from blue's shows and from the maps of today's engine, each with its id, and the code they live in. The card's head counts those findings, names the questions it answers where there are any, marks a problem that was seen live, and names any fix on blue it came from as a clue.

The standalone games section restates decision 22 and the two biggest gaps with no engine, with the hardware scanner's parity table folded under it. The evidence at the end gives the totals, the findings set aside with their reasons, and where each flaw lives in today's code. Nothing on the candidate side is decided; step 3 puts competing designs in front of you.
